theme: Test the spirits; God is love; assurance
readingInstruction: Read 1 John 4:1-5:21. John gives more tests, including testing the spirits, and reaches the heights in his teaching on God’s love. The letter ends with a statement of its purpose: that you may know that you have eternal life.
settingTheScene: In these chapters John returns to the tests of true faith: believing that Jesus has come in the flesh, loving one another, and obeying God’s commands. He is concerned about false prophets who deny the incarnation. He lays out the foundation of Christian love in the character of God and the love of Christ. The letter closes with assurance and the confidence that believers can pray according to God’s will.
observation: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (4:1).
“Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love” (4:8).
“In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10).
“There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (4:18).
“We love because he first loved us” (4:19).
“For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome” (5:3).
“I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13).
interpretation:
John tells his readers to test every spirit, because many false prophets are in the world. The test is confessing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Anyone who denies this is the spirit of the antichrist. But “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.” This is the first central theme: truth.

The second theme is love. “Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.” This is not just a description of God’s feelings; it is who he is. And where do we see this love? “In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” Love begins with God, not with us. And “if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” No one has ever seen God, but if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us. The Spirit he has given us is the assurance that we abide in him.

Verse 18 is a comfort: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.” When we are sure of the Father’s love, we do not fear final punishment. And then the memory verse of the unit: “We love because he first loved us.” Our love is a response. And finally the test: “If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.”

Chapter 5 states that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. Love for God means keeping his commandments, “and his commandments are not burdensome. For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world.” The victory is our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? John then speaks of the three witnesses: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, which agree. Most interpreters understand these as Jesus’ baptism, his death on the cross, and the Spirit’s testimony. (Some older English translations include an additional clause about “the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” in verse 7, which is not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts.)

The great purpose statement: “And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God that you may know that you have eternal life.” Assurance is possible, and it is what the whole letter aims at. He then gives confidence in prayer: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.” There is mention of a “sin that leads to death” (5:16-17), which interpreters take differently: a persistent, public rejection of Christ, or apostasy, or a sin bringing physical death. The point is that we should pray for our brothers, and that all wrongdoing is sin. We know that everyone born of God does not keep on sinning, that the Son of God keeps him, and that the evil one does not touch him. The final words, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols,” are a call to cling to the true God.
connection: Deuteronomy 13:1-5 and 1 Corinthians 12:3 speak of testing prophets. Romans 5:8 and John 3:16 are other statements of God’s love. Exodus 34:6-7 declares God’s steadfast love. Romans 8:15 says we have not received a spirit of fear but of adoption. Matthew 22:36-40 joins loving God and neighbor. John 14:15 says if you love me, you will keep my commandments. Matthew 11:30 speaks of an easy yoke. John 16:33 says Christ has overcome the world. John 20:31 states a similar purpose. Hebrews 6:4-8 and 10:26-31 relate to the sin leading to death. Exodus 20:3-5 forbids idols.
application:
Think of a teaching you recently heard. Test it by what it says about Christ.

Read 4:9-10 again. Whom do you find difficult to love? Ask God to help you love them as he has loved you.

Write down 5:13 on a card and keep it where you see it as a reminder that you can know you have eternal life.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is love and sent his Son.
Ask him to help you love because he first loved you.
Ask him to strengthen your assurance.
